# PDS Crate (Custos)

Last verified: 2026-07-13

## Purpose

The PDS is the axum-based web server. It is the sole Imperative Shell in the workspace —
the only crate that touches SQLite, handles HTTP, or manages process-level state. All other
crates (`crypto`, `repo-engine`, `common`) are pure Functional Cores that the PDS calls.

## Module Map

```
src/
  main.rs          — startup: open pool, run migrations, bind server
  telemetry.rs     — OTel tracing-subscriber init (`init_subscriber`) + shutdown-flushing `OtelGuard`; wired by main.rs at startup, dropped after graceful shutdown. `[telemetry] log_format = "json"` switches the stdout fmt layer to one-JSON-object-per-line
  metrics.rs       — OTel meter + Prometheus registry behind `GET /metrics` (see "Metrics" section below): typed `Metrics` handle in AppState, instrument/label name constants (`metrics::names`), the `http_requests_total` middleware, and the `SubscriberGuard` RAII gauge
  app.rs           — router construction (route table + shared middleware layers); re-exports `AppState`/`FailedLoginStore` (and, under `#[cfg(test)]`, `test_state`/`test_state_with_plc_url`) from `state.rs` so the ~120 existing `crate::app::AppState` imports across the crate stay unchanged
  state.rs         — `AppState` definition + `FailedLoginStore`, plus the `#[cfg(test)]` `test_state`/`test_state_with_plc_url` constructors
```

### `firehose/`

The **persistent** event pipeline behind `com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos`, split into three
cohesive layers so the subtle invariant-heavy staging code is reviewable in isolation. `mod.rs`
re-exports every submodule's public types (`Firehose`, `FirehoseEvent`, `CommitInput`, `Subscription`,
etc.) at `crate::firehose::*`, so the 19 consumer files address them exactly as before the split.

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `mod.rs` | `Firehose` (the durable sequencer + broadcast fan-out), the bare `emit_commit`/`emit_account`/`emit_identity`/`emit_sync` primitives, and the atomic staged-transaction path (`lock_emit`/`EmitGuard`/`PendingCommit`/`PendingAccount`/`PendingWithSync`) — the emit-lock/staging invariants documented below |
| `events.rs` | The wire-facing event model (`RepoOp`, `CommitEvent`, `AccountEvent`, `IdentityEvent`, `SyncEvent`, `FirehoseEvent`), their DAG-CBOR stored-payload encoding, `decode_stored_event` (reconstructs an event from a persisted `repo_seq` row for replay), and the pre-persist wire-CID/CAR-size validation. Pure data + (de)serialization, no `Firehose` state |
| `replay.rs` | Cursor replay over the durable log: `Subscription`/`SubscribeOutcome` (the subscribe handshake) and `ReplayReader` (paged `(cursor, upper]` replay with the best-effort-vs-fail-closed pruning logic) |

The module holds a durable
monotonic sequencer (backed by the `repo_seq` table, V028) and a Tokio `broadcast` channel;
`AppState.firehose: Arc<Firehose>` is shared by every handler. Each repo commit calls
`record_write::commit_repo_write`, which builds the commit's block diff
(`repo_engine::collect_commit_diff` — one walk of the new root, yielding both the `added` diff
blocks and the `new_reachable` keep-set — + `build_car_from_cids`, run *before* post-commit GC) and
publishes a sequenced `CommitEvent` carrying the DID, rev, `since`, `prevData` (the previous
commit's MST root CID — Sync v1.1's inductive-validation anchor, captured before the write mutates
the repo; `None` for genesis), per-record `RepoOp`s (action + collection/rkey + cid + prev + value;
`prev` is the previous record CID for an update/delete — Sync v1.1's per-op inductive-validation
anchor — `None` for a create), and
the CARv1 diff blocks. The `#commit` wire frame emits the deprecated `blobs` list empty. Backpressure is by design: the bounded
channel never blocks producers — a slow subscriber observes `Lagged` and is expected to disconnect.
All three write paths (`create_record`/`put_record` via `record_write`, `delete_record`,
`apply_writes`) emit exactly one event per commit. (Those same write paths reject a deactivated
account with 403 before committing.) `create_did.rs`'s `promote_account` stages the same kind of
`#commit` event for a new account's *genesis* repo, atomically with the `accounts`/`did_documents`/
`sessions` inserts, so a fresh host self-announces to the relay instead of staying invisible until
its first record write; chained after that genesis `#commit` in the same transaction is a Sync v1.1
`#sync` state assertion (via `PendingCommit::stage_sync`, carrying a single-root CAR of just the
signed commit block), so a relay can anchor to this fresh host's head. It then emits a best-effort
`#account` (active) frame and calls `crawlers.notify()` once that transaction has committed.
A `#sync` frame (`SyncEvent`: DID, rev, and a ≤10 KB commit-block CAR) is the Sync v1.1 head
assertion relays use to auto-repair drift; it is emitted on account genesis (above) and on
`activateAccount` (chained after the `#account` via `PendingAccount::stage_sync` when the account
has a repo — the commit-block CAR is built *before* the transaction, since the single-connection
pool can't serve a block read while the tx holds the connection). `importRepo` (shipped,
`routes/import_repo.rs`) deliberately does *not* emit one — a migrated repo's head assertion rides
on the `activateAccount` that follows it in the migration sequence. Account-status changes emit a separate
`#account` frame instead of a `#commit`: `activate_account.rs`/`deactivate_account.rs` stage one
via `Firehose::stage_account` (active=false/`deactivated` or active=true) **only on a real status
transition** — a redundant no-op activate/deactivate returns 200 and emits nothing.
`update_subject_status.rs` (`com.atproto.admin.updateSubjectStatus`) stages the same kind of frame
for an admin-driven takedown/clear, but derives `active`/`status` from the account's full
`AccountLifecycle` after the write rather than assuming its own dimension won — clearing a
takedown on a still-suspended account must report `suspended`, not `active`. The `#account` frame
shares the same sequencer so account frames are ordered relative to commits.

**Durability and atomicity.** `Firehose::emit_commit`/`emit_account`/`emit_identity`/`emit_sync`
persist each event to
`repo_seq` (via `db::firehose_seq`) **before** broadcasting it, all under one async `emit_lock`
that keeps broadcast order = `seq` order and the log a dense prefix (a failed insert doesn't
consume a `seq`). The sequencer loads `MAX(seq)` on construction, so `seq` is monotonic across
restarts/redeploys. Those methods remain bare best-effort primitives — used directly by tests,
`emit_identity`'s neighbours (`create_handle.rs`/`delete_handle.rs`/`update_handle.rs`), and
`create_did.rs`'s post-commit `emit_account` call, none of which need atomicity with a specific
transaction; the call sites that do instead acquire `emit_lock` via `Firehose::lock_emit`
(returning an `EmitGuard`) *before* opening their transaction, then call
`EmitGuard::stage_commit`/`stage_account` to insert the `repo_seq` row into that *caller's own*
open transaction. A caller that also needs a chained `#sync` in the same transaction (genesis,
activation) calls `PendingCommit::stage_sync`/`PendingAccount::stage_sync`, which inserts the
`#sync` row at the next `seq` and returns a `PendingWithSync` whose `finish` broadcasts the primary
event then the `#sync`, advancing the counter past both. The staging insert lands in the caller's
open transaction — the same one carrying the repo-root CAS (`record_write::commit_repo_write`,
`create_did.rs`'s genesis promotion) or the account-status UPDATE (`activate_account`/
`deactivate_account`) — and get back a `Pending*` handle that carries the guard forward. Acquiring
the lock before the transaction (rather than inside the staging call) matters on this crate's
single-connection pool: `emit_commit`/
`emit_account`/`emit_identity` already acquire the lock before touching the pool, so a staging
path that instead opened its transaction first and acquired the lock after could deadlock against
one of them (each would hold what the other is waiting for). The caller commits that transaction
and only then calls `Pending*::finish` to advance `last_seq` and broadcast; a failed insert rolls
the whole transaction back (via `?`/`Drop`) rather than landing the state change with a
silently-dropped event, and dropping a `Pending*` without finishing never advances the sequence,
so the seq is retried by the next emit. The one asymmetric drop — a handler future cancelled
(client disconnect) *after* its `tx.commit()` made the staged row durable but before `finish` —
leaves `last_seq` behind the durable log; every insert goes through
`Firehose::insert_at_frontier`, which detects the resulting PRIMARY KEY collision, re-derives the
frontier from the durable `MAX(seq)`, and retries once, so one cancelled request costs one
never-broadcast event (still replayable from the log, like any pre-restart event) instead of
wedging all writes until restart. `subscribe_from(cursor)` snapshots the live receiver and
the sequence frontier `upper` together under
`emit_lock`; the `sync_subscribe_repos` handler then pages the durable log for `(cursor, upper]`
(`events_in_range`, decoded via `decode_stored_event`) and streams live events (`seq > upper`)
after — the two ranges are exactly disjoint, so the replay→live boundary has no gap and no
duplication, and replay now survives a restart (it reads the log, not an in-memory buffer). The
subscriber-facing WebSocket frame encoding lives in the `sync_subscribe_repos` handler.

### `crawler.rs`

Outbound `com.atproto.sync.requestCrawl` notifier. `AppState.crawlers: Arc<CrawlerNotifier>`
is shared by every handler. The re-invitation fires from three places: **(1)** on startup
(`main.rs` calls `crawlers.notify()` once when crawlers are configured — a fresh deploy is exactly
when a dropped relay subscription must be re-invited); **(2)** on **every firehose emission**, via
`Firehose::broadcast` (the single fan-out choke point), which the notifier is attached to at boot
(`attach_crawlers`) — so `#commit` **and** the `#account`/`#identity`/`#sync` lifecycle frames all
re-invite the relay, not just repo commits; **(3)** the same broadcast path covers `create_did.rs`/
`create_account_xrpc.rs`/`agent_child.rs`, which additionally call `notify()` directly after their
own commit path. `notify` is fire-and-forget: it selects the crawlers outside their rate-limit
window (one notification per crawler per 30s), then spawns a detached task per crawler that POSTs
`{ "hostname": <PDS-host> }` to `<url>/xrpc/com.atproto.sync.requestCrawl`, retrying with
exponential backoff up to 3 times. All outcomes are logged, never propagated — an emission never
blocks on or fails because of a crawler. Configured via `[crawlers] urls = [...]` (default
`["https://bsky.network"]`; empty disables) or `EZPDS_CRAWLERS`.

Why notify on non-commit frames matters: a relay can silently drop its subscription to a quiet
PDS, and if the PDS only re-invited on commits, a post-migration `#account`(active)/`#sync` burst
emitted while nobody was listening would leave the network's last word on the DID as the source
PDS's deactivation — the DID stuck `AccountDeactivated` network-wide until a repo write happens to
fire another `requestCrawl`. Emitting on the lifecycle frames closes that gap; the durable
`repo_seq` log means the relay's replay heals everything once it reconnects (within retention).

### `relay_status.rs`

The **inbound** half of federation health, complementing `crawler.rs`'s outbound `requestCrawl`:
a `com.atproto.sync.getHostStatus` client that asks the configured relay what it knows about this
PDS. Backs `GET /v1/admin/relay-status` (route `admin_relay_status.rs`), the operator's "is my
server actually federating right now" readout. `fetch_host_status` returns a `RelayReport`:
`Found(HostStatus{ seq, account_count, status })` (the relay's cursor into *our* firehose seq-space,
how many of our accounts it has indexed, and the lifecycle status it assigns us), `NotFound` (the
relay is up but has never crawled us — a normal "not federating yet" state, distinct from an
outage), or `Unreachable(reason)` (transport failure, timeout, non-2xx, or unparseable body). It is
**total, never fatal** — every failure path becomes a variant rather than an `Err`, so the admin
readout always renders the literal truth of what the relay said.

The gap the readout reports is `pdsHeadSeq − relaySeq`, and `pdsHeadSeq` is our **exact** sequencer
head (`firehose.current_seq()`): because we own the PDS, the route reads the head directly instead
of the timed-`subscribeRepos` approximation a third-party observer must make. This module only
fetches the relay's side; `admin_relay_status.rs` does the compare. Like `admin_health.rs`, the
route reports raw truth only — the ok/warn/behind verdict (gap thresholds, status mapping) lives
with the operator (the companion app's relay-status block), never in the API shape. The `#[serde]`
status string is kept verbatim (not an enum) so an unknown value from a newer relay is passed
through rather than dropped. `POST /v1/admin/request-crawl` (route `admin_request_crawl.rs`) is the
companion action: the operator "Request crawl" button, driving `CrawlerNotifier::request_crawl_now`
to re-invite every configured relay immediately (bypassing the 30s auto-notify window) and reporting
each relay's outcome.

### `rate_limit.rs`

Reference-parity request rate limiting. The pure sliding-window algorithm (`MultiWindowLimiter`,
supporting several windows per key with weighted "points") lives in `auth/rate_limit.rs` (Functional
Core); this module is the Imperative Shell that owns the process-level `Mutex`-wrapped limiters and
the Axum middleware. Three families, all off when `[rate_limit] enabled = false` (the test harness
sets this):

1. **Global per-IP** — 1 point/request keyed by client IP (leftmost `X-Forwarded-For`, else the TCP
   peer), default 3000/5min. `com.atproto.sync.getRepo`, `subscribeRepos`, and `_health` are exempt
   so relay backfill/firehose and platform health checks are never throttled.
2. **Per-endpoint per-IP** — tighter caps on `createAccount`/`createSession` (password and
   sovereign session creation share one budget)/`resetPassword`/
   `updateHandle` (plus the native `/v1/accounts[/mobile]` signup routes), `/v1/transfer/accept`
   (authenticated by a bare 6-char code, so a short-code endpoint belongs here by default), and
   the agent claim-ceremony pair `/agent/identity/claim/confirm` + `/v1/agents/claim-preview`
   (both validate a guessable 6-digit `user_code`; they **share one limiter instance** so
   alternating endpoints can't double the guess budget), and the escrow-recovery pair
   `/v1/recovery/initiate` + `/v1/recovery/release` (the release endpoint validates an emailed
   OTP; both **share one limiter instance** so alternating can't double the OTP-guess budget),
   keyed by IP.
3. **Per-account write points** — create=3/update=2/delete=1 over an hourly + daily window, charged
   in `record_write::commit_repo_write` (the single choke point for all four repo-write routes),
   keyed by the **authenticated** DID. Keying on the verified DID — not an unverified token subject —
   is deliberate: otherwise anyone could drain a victim's budget.

Rejections return `429` with the standard error envelope plus `RateLimit-Limit`/`-Remaining`/
`-Reset` and `Retry-After`; successful requests carry the `RateLimit-*` headers of the tightest
applicable limiter. All knobs are configurable via `[rate_limit]` in `pds.toml` / `EZPDS_RATE_LIMIT_*`
(a knob of `0` disables that specific limiter).

### `iroh_tunnel.rs`

The Iroh QUIC tunnel — a NAT-traversing endpoint devices dial by node id instead of by a
routable address. Opt-in via `[iroh] enabled` (default off); when enabled, `main.rs` loads the
persistent node identity (`auth::load_or_create_iroh_secret_key`, backed by the `iroh_identity`
table so the node id is stable across restarts), binds the endpoint with the `N0` preset (n0
discovery + relays), and spawns a detached accept loop. `[iroh] ipv6` (default true;
`EZPDS_IROH_IPV6`) gates the IPv6 QUIC socket: on a v4-only host (e.g. a Railway container with
no public v6 egress) set it false, and `start` clears the pre-configured IP transports and
re-binds IPv4 only — without it iroh's v6 relay probes fail `NetworkUnreachable` forever, one
WARN every ~80s that buries real errors. `AppState.iroh: Option<Arc<IrohState>>`
holds the bound endpoint and its node-id string; `get_device_pds` advertises that node id.
The accept loop speaks a minimal v0.1 echo protocol on the `ezpds/iroh/0` ALPN — enough to
prove the bidirectional channel and serve as a liveness probe; the real repo-sync / push
protocols register here later. Errors are logged, never propagated (one bad peer never stops
the loop). The endpoint is closed on graceful shutdown, which ends the accept loop.

### `read_after_write/`

**Read-after-write:** Buffered munge path for six munged AppView NSIDs
(`app.bsky.feed.getTimeline`, `getAuthorFeed`, `getPostThread`, `getActorLikes`,
`app.bsky.actor.getProfile`, `getProfiles`). Merges the requester's unindexed records
(fetched from the firehose event log via `get_records_since_rev`) into the AppView's indexed
response. Selects records by comparing the AppView's `atproto-repo-rev` header to the account's
current repo CID (`repo_seq`): records with `indexed_at` timestamps *after* the AppView's rev
are included. The core `pipethrough_munged` handler implements the full fallback ladder:
(1) upstream error → return error unchanged; (2) non-2xx → return buffered original (except
`getPostThread` 400 NotFound, which triggers reconstruction); (3) JSON parse error → return buffered
original; (4) empty LocalRecords → return buffered original with NO lag header; (5) munge/hydration
errors → log and return buffered original (fallback to untouched upstream response). Response buffering
is capped at 10 MiB; oversized responses trigger early bailout. The `Atproto-Upstream-Lag` header
(milliseconds since the oldest merged record's indexed_at) is set only when local.count > 0.
Submodules:

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `mod.rs` | `pipethrough_munged` handler, fallback ladder, buffering cap, response error handling, lag header calculation |
| `munge.rs` | Per-NSID munges `get_timeline`, `get_author_feed`, `get_post_thread`, `get_actor_likes`, `get_profile`, `get_profiles` — injection/overwriting of the requester's records. `// pattern: Mixed (unavoidable)` (the feed/thread munges orchestrate async hydration through `LocalViewer`) |
| `viewer.rs` | `LocalViewer`: hydrates local records as feed items / profile views with author/counts populated via AppView prefetch, renders quote embeds with appview-fetched URIs (falls back to `#viewNotFound` on errors) |
| `types.rs` | `LocalRecords`, `RecordDescript` — structured container for unindexed records bucket by collection |

The munge path shares `service_proxy::proxy_request` extraction with the streaming fast path
(both mint service auth, both buffer request bodies up to MAX_PROXY_BODY, both forward query params,
both forward the same request/response header subsets — see `service_proxy.rs`'s
`REQ_HEADERS_TO_FORWARD`/`forward_response_headers`).
`mint_service_auth` is `pub(crate)` so `pipethrough_munged` can re-use the JWT minting logic.
Every rung of the fallback ladder returns through the module's `passthrough_response` helper, so a
degraded response still carries the upstream's `atproto-content-labelers`/`atproto-repo-rev`.

**Config:** The AppView is configured via `[appview]` in `pds.toml` (`EZPDS_APPVIEW_URL` env var,
default `https://api.bsky.app`) and `EZPDS_APPVIEW_DID` (default `did:web:api.bsky.app#bsky_appview`).
The optional `EZPDS_APPVIEW_CDN_URL` (default `https://cdn.bsky.app`) overrides the blob CDN
endpoint in blob embed URLs (useful for egress-heavy testing with a local blobstore).

**Rule:** `db/` submodules never import from `routes/` or `auth/`. They accept `&SqlitePool`
and return data; callers decide what to do with it.

### `routes/`

One file per HTTP endpoint. Each handler is a thin Imperative Shell:
**gather** (extract state/body/headers) → **process** (call `auth/` or `db/`) → **respond**.

| File | Endpoint |
|---|---|
| `oauth_authorize.rs` | `GET/POST /oauth/authorize` |
| `oauth_par.rs` | `POST /oauth/par` — for discoverable (https URL) client_ids, a private-use-scheme redirect_uri must be the client_id host's reverse-FQDN (`invalid_redirect_uri` otherwise), matching bsky.social's enforcement of the atproto OAuth rule |
| `oauth_token/` | `POST /oauth/token` — one route module split across per-grant submodules: `mod.rs` (request/response types, the shared token-issuance + `cleanup_expired_state` helpers, and the `post_token` grant dispatcher) plus `authorization_code.rs`, `refresh.rs`, `jwt_bearer.rs`, and `claim_polling.rs` (each grant's distinct logic + error surface, and its tests). Still a single route module, so the no-routes-importing-routes rule is untouched. Grants: `authorization_code` + `refresh_token` (DPoP-bound, rotating refresh tokens), `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer` (RFC 7523), and `urn:workos:agent-auth:grant-type:claim` (auth.md Step 4c). **jwt-bearer** exchanges a service-signed agent `identity_assertion` for a short-lived **Bearer** access token (no DPoP, no refresh token; the agent identity must be `claimed` with a DID matching the assertion `sub` — unclaimed/absent → `invalid_grant`, `revoked` → `access_denied`, non-origin `resource` → `invalid_target`). The issued token carries the assertion's granular `scope` verbatim (no widening: the grant accepts no requested `scope`) **and** its `registration_id` claim, which marks the token agent-derived (see `auth/extractors.rs::AuthenticatedUser::{is_agent,require_not_agent}`) and ties it to the `agent_identities` row for revocation/audit. **Revocation is bounded by the access-token TTL:** flipping an identity to `revoked` blocks the *next* exchange immediately, but an already-issued access token stays valid until it expires (5 min); there is no live-token revocation list. **claim-polling** is the machine-pollable half of the claim ceremony: a `service_auth`/`anonymous` agent polls with its one-time `claim_token` (no DPoP — it may hold no key yet; the token is the credential) while the owner confirms out-of-band. Reads the identity's lifecycle state and reports it as OAuth device-flow codes — `authorization_pending` (active, ceremony still pending), `expired_token` (`claim_token`/`user_code` window lapsed), `access_denied` (`revoked`), or **200** with a fresh Bearer token + the stored post-claim `identity_assertion` (+ `assertion_expires`) once `claimed` (scope derived from the row's stored scopes, so it matches a jwt-bearer exchange of the same assertion byte-for-byte). Polling faster than the advertised `interval` (`auth/agent_assertion.rs::POLL_INTERVAL_SECS`, 5s) → `slow_down`, throttled by the in-memory `AppState.poll_tracker` keyed by the `claim_token`'s SHA-256 (never the raw secret; pruned in `cleanup_expired_state`) |

Auth is DPoP proof-of-possession like the `refresh_token` grant: the proof's key thumbprint must match the token's bound `jkt` (and, when the caller names a `client_id`, its owning client), so a party that only observed the token string can't revoke it — closing the RFC 7009 DoS-oracle concern. Every well-formed, DPoP-authenticated request returns **200 with an empty body** regardless of whether a token matched (RFC 7009 §2.2 non-disclosure); only a missing `token` (`invalid_request`) or a missing/invalid DPoP proof (`invalid_dpop_proof`/`use_dpop_nonce`) returns the `{error, error_description}` shape. Whenever the header **is** present, on any of the three namespaces, `app.rs::xrpc_handler` resolves it via `identity::resolution::resolve_atproto_proxy_target` (`did#serviceId` → DID document → matching `service` entry's `serviceEndpoint`) and routes there instead — this is what lets the official app's `app.bsky.video.*` calls, sent with `atproto-proxy: did:web:video.bsky.app#bsky_video`, reach the video service rather than the AppView; a missing header on moderation is 400, an unresolvable target is 503. Since that target DID is caller-controlled, the resolved `serviceEndpoint` is always SSRF-guarded (`identity::resolution::validate_proxy_endpoint`) on this path, regardless of namespace: rejects non-http(s) schemes, userinfo, query/fragment, and any host — IP literal or DNS-resolved — that isn't a public address (loopback/private/link-local incl. cloud-metadata/unique-local-IPv6/etc.). The caller-controlled request is sent on the shared `state.hardened_http_client` (`proxy_request`'s `caller_controlled_target` branch), whose `SsrfResolver` re-applies that allowlist to any domain resolution at connect time, so a second DNS answer can't substitute an unchecked address. The six **read-after-write NSIDs** (`app.bsky.feed.{getTimeline,getAuthorFeed,getPostThread,getActorLikes}` + `app.bsky.actor.{getProfile,getProfiles}`) route to `read_after_write::pipethrough_munged` (buffered munge path: merges requester's unindexed records, applies fallback ladder, emits `Atproto-Upstream-Lag` header) only when **no** header is present — the munge path hardcodes the configured AppView internally, so an explicit header bypasses it and streams to the header target via `proxy_xrpc` instead; all other unmunged `app.bsky.*` NSIDs always stream through `proxy_xrpc` (fast path: no buffering). `chat.bsky.*` requires full access or a *privileged* app password regardless of target (plain `com.atproto.appPass` refused with 403). Both paths share `proxy_request` extraction (`mint_service_auth` is `pub(crate)`) **and** the header-forwarding seam, which is reference-parity with the upstream PDS's pipethrough: `REQ_HEADERS_TO_FORWARD` (`accept-language`, `atproto-accept-labelers`, `x-bsky-topics`) is copied onto the outbound request, and `forward_response_headers` copies `RES_HEADERS_TO_FORWARD` (`atproto-repo-rev`, `atproto-content-labelers`, `retry-after`) back onto the client response — on the streaming path and on **every rung** of the munge path's fallback ladder, so the headers a client sees never depend on which path or rung served it. `atproto-accept-labelers` is load-bearing: the AppView applies only the labelers the caller names there (defaulting to its own moderation service alone when absent), so dropping it silently strips every subscribed labeler's labels from posts and profiles. |

## Metrics

The federation-health instrument set served by `GET /metrics`. Names and label keys are
constants in `metrics::names` — **this table mirrors that module; change them together.**
Counters are constructed *without* the `_total` suffix (the Prometheus exporter appends it;
a unit test in `metrics.rs` pins the rendered names). All instruments record through the
typed `AppState.metrics` handle; when `[telemetry] metrics_enabled = false` the same handle
drops measurements at the SDK boundary, so call sites never branch.

never from request data (raw URIs, rkeys, DIDs, hostnames).

## Hard Rules

**Routes must not import from other routes.**
If two routes share logic, that logic belongs in `auth/` (pure) or `db/` (queries). A route
importing from another route creates hidden coupling and makes it impossible to reason about
a handler in isolation.

**Every `.rs` file with runtime behavior must have a pattern comment.**
Add `// pattern: Functional Core`, `// pattern: Imperative Shell`, or
`// pattern: Mixed (unavoidable)` at the top of any file containing functions or
orchestration logic. Files with only types, constants, or re-exports are exempt.

**`db/` submodules own queries, not transactions.**
Business-logic transactions (multi-table atomic operations) live in the route handler or
a dedicated helper called by the handler — not inside `db/` functions. `db/` functions
accept `&SqlitePool` or `&mut SqliteTransaction`; they never open transactions themselves
unless the operation is inherently single-table.

**Authentication must never be cookie-based; permissive CORS on the public surface depends on it.**
`app.rs` applies `CorsLayer::permissive()` to the public surface (landing, `.well-known`, OAuth,
agent registration, all XRPC, static assets) but deliberately **not** to the admin/provisioning
`/v1/*` surface (same-origin only). Permissive CORS is safe only because every auth path is
Bearer/DPoP/signed-request — never an ambient cookie — so a hostile origin cannot ride a logged-in
user's credentials. If any future auth mechanism becomes cookie-based, the permissive CORS layer
must be tightened (explicit origin allowlist + credentials handling) in the same change.

## Adding a New Route

1. Create `src/routes/<name>.rs` with `// pattern: Imperative Shell` at the top.
2. If the handler needs shared auth logic → add to `auth/` (pure) or use an existing extractor.
3. If the handler needs a new DB query → add to the appropriate `db/` submodule.
4. If it's an XRPC procedure: a JSON input body is parsed with `LexiconInput<T>` (never bare
   `axum::Json<T>`) after vendoring its lexicon document (`crates/pds/lexicons/README.md`); a
   no-input procedure takes `NoInputBody` instead. Both must be the handler's final extractor.
5. Register in `src/app.rs` router.
6. Add a `.bru` file in `bruno/` (see root AGENTS.md).

## Adding a New DB Query

1. Identify the owning entity (`accounts`, `oauth`, etc.).
2. Add the function to the matching `db/<entity>.rs` file.
3. If no matching file exists, create one with `// pattern: Imperative Shell`.
4. Export the function and any new data struct via `db/mod.rs` (`pub mod <entity>;`).

content.thinking:
I've confirmed that wallet migrations create accounts without any password field, leaving `password_hash` as NULL. Now I'm checking whether did:web accounts should have sovereign sessions—for did:plc, sovereignty comes from the PLC rotation key set on plc.directory, so for did:web the equivalent authority would be the verification methods in the DID document served from the domain's `.well-known/did.json` endpoint.

But there's a complication: if Custos itself hosts the did.json for opted-in accounts, then verifying against that document becomes circular—Custos would be checking a document it serves and the account can modify. And critically, the `#atproto` repo signing key is held by the PDS itself, not the wallet, so that's not sovereign either, unlike did:plc where rotation keys are wallet-controlled and separate from the repo signing key.

The real issue is that did:web has no rotation key concept at all—the verification methods in the DID document are the only analogue, but on Custos-migrated accounts the only one present is `#atproto`, which the PDS controls. So a straightforward "sign with a key from the did doc" approach wouldn't actually be sovereign.

I need to check whether the wallet adds its own key to the did.json during migration, and look at the migration test and any design docs about did:web sovereign sessions to see if this gap is already known.

1	# ADR-0022: `did:web` for user-owned domains
2	
3	- **Status:** Accepted
4	- **Date:** 2026-07-13
5	- **Deciders:** ezpds maintainers
6	- **Related:** [ADR-0001](0001-client-held-rotation-key-custody.md) · [ADR-0003](0003-did-plc-as-did-method.md) · [MM-278](https://linear.app/atbb/issue/MM-278) · [MM-279](https://linear.app/atbb/issue/MM-279) · [MM-285](https://linear.app/atbb/issue/MM-285)
7	
8	## Context
9	
10	ADR-0003 made `did:plc` the only account identity method because its ordered rotation keys and
11	72-hour recovery window support client-held custody. That remains the strongest default, but it
12	also excluded identities whose root of trust is intentionally a user-owned domain. Custos can
13	support those identities without claiming that domain control has PLC's recovery semantics.
14	
15	Serving a DID for a domain the user does not control would create indefinite exit liability. A
16	new or migrated `did:web` therefore needs an external proof that the wallet-approved document is
17	already authoritative at the user's domain before Custos creates the account or takes over hosting.
18	
19	## Decision
20	
21	Custos may mint, migrate, or host a `did:web` identity only for a user-owned domain, after the
22	wallet proves control by publishing the exact reviewed DID document at its authoritative HTTPS
23	URL. `did:plc` remains the default identity method.
24	
25	The document publishes the wallet device key alongside Custos's reserved `#atproto` key and
26	`#atproto_pds` service. The existing 2-of-3 escrow restores the device key, not domain ownership.
27	Custos-hosted updates require device-key approval; self-hosted identities use that key as a
28	monitoring anchor. DNS remains the immediate override and exit boundary.
29	
30	Wallet recovery language and controls are method-specific. PLC monitoring, fork-point recovery,
31	and the 72-hour override apply only to `did:plc`; `did:web` recovery is domain control plus
32	escrowed keys.
33	
34	## Consequences
35	
36	- Users can create or migrate all four new/existing and self/Custos-hosted `did:web` shapes.
37	- Account promotion performs an SSRF-hardened external fetch and exact byte comparison; it never
38	  submits a PLC operation.
39	- Domain compromise remains identity compromise. Device-key escrow restores co-signing and
40	  monitoring continuity but cannot replace domain control.
41	- Custos accepts hosting liability only after independently observable proof of user control, and
42	  users can exit by repointing DNS.
43	- Method-specific UI and recovery paths must remain gated so `did:web` never inherits PLC claims.
44	
45	## Alternatives considered
46	
47	- **Keep `did:plc` as the only method.** Rejected because it prevents users from choosing domain
48	  control as their identity root and blocks migration of existing `did:web` accounts.
49	- **Mint `did:web` before publication.** Rejected because an authenticated wallet session does not
50	  prove control of the named domain.
51	- **Host domains Custos controls on a user's behalf.** Rejected because identity ownership and
52	  exit would remain dependent on Custos.

72-hour recovery window support client-held custody. That remains the strongest default, but it
also excluded identities whose root of trust is intentionally a user-owned domain. Custos can
support those identities without claiming that domain control has PLC's recovery semantics.

Serving a DID for a domain the user does not control would create indefinite exit liability. A
new or migrated `did:web` therefore needs an external proof that the wallet-approved document is
already authoritative at the user's domain before Custos creates the account or takes over hosting.

## Decision

Custos may mint, migrate, or host a `did:web` identity only for a user-owned domain, after the
wallet proves control by publishing the exact reviewed DID document at its authoritative HTTPS
URL. `did:plc` remains the default identity method.

The document publishes the wallet device key alongside Custos's reserved `#atproto` key and
`#atproto_pds` service. The existing 2-of-3 escrow restores the device key, not domain ownership.
Custos-hosted updates require device-key approval; self-hosted identities use that key as a
monitoring anchor. DNS remains the immediate override and exit boundary.

Wallet recovery language and controls are method-specific. PLC monitoring, fork-point recovery,
and the 72-hour override apply only to `did:plc`; `did:web` recovery is domain control plus
escrowed keys.

## Consequences

- Users can create or migrate all four new/existing and self/Custos-hosted `did:web` shapes.
- Account promotion performs an SSRF-hardened external fetch and exact byte comparison; it never
  submits a PLC operation.
- Domain compromise remains identity compromise. Device-key escrow restores co-signing and
  monitoring continuity but cannot replace domain control.
- Custos accepts hosting liability only after independently observable proof of user control, and
  users can exit by repointing DNS.
- Method-specific UI and recovery paths must remain gated so `did:web` never inherits PLC claims.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep `did:plc` as the only method.** Rejected because it prevents users from choosing domain
  control as their identity root and blocks migration of existing `did:web` accounts.
- **Mint `did:web` before publication.** Rejected because an authenticated wallet session does not
  prove control of the named domain.
- **Host domains Custos controls on a user's behalf.** Rejected because identity ownership and
  exit would remain dependent on Custos.

content.text:
## Short answer

**No — there was no password step, and there couldn't have been.** The wallet's migration `createAccount` request literally has no `password` field:

```rust
// apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/pds_client.rs:537
pub struct CreateAccountMigrationRequest {
    pub handle: String,
    pub email: String,
    pub did: String,
    pub invite_code: Option<String>,
}
```

and the server side deliberately accepts that — [create_account_xrpc.rs:507](crates/pds/src/routes/create_account_xrpc.rs:507):

```rust
// A migration account may carry no password (OAuth-only); store NULL then.
```

So `did:web:malpercio.dev` landed with `password_hash = NULL`, exactly as your peek at `accounts` suggested. That's by design for did:plc accounts, because they have a passwordless path. did:web doesn't.

## Why the OAuth login is failing

There are exactly two ways to complete `/oauth/authorize`, and your account qualifies for neither:

1. **Password consent form** — [oauth_authorize.rs:707](crates/pds/src/routes/oauth_authorize.rs:707):
   ```rust
   let verify_result = match account.password_hash.as_deref() {
       None | Some("") => VerifyResult::WrongPassword,
       Some(h) => verify_password(h, &password),
   };
   ```
   NULL password is folded into "wrong password" so it isn't an enumeration oracle. You get "Invalid credentials" no matter what you type.

2. **Wallet-confirmed consent** (the passwordless path built for exactly this lockout) — [oauth_consent.rs:252](crates/pds/src/routes/oauth_consent.rs:252):
   ```rust
   if !is_plc_did(&request.did) { ... }
   ```
   Hard-gated to `did:plc:`. Same gate in [sovereign_session.rs:114](crates/pds/src/routes/sovereign_session.rs:114).

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The gate isn't arbitrary caution — it's structural. Both passwordless paths verify the approval signature against `fetch_current_plc_state(...).rotation_keys`, i.e. **plc.directory's authoritative audit log**, explicitly *not* the cached DID doc. did:web has no rotation-key concept and no audit log, so there is simply nothing for that code to call. The gate is where the abstraction ran out, not a policy decision that was written down.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Immediate unblock:** `requestPasswordReset` → `resetPassword` works on a NULL-password account (no passwordless guard in either route; `update_password_hash` is a plain UPDATE). Note the *admin* repair route refuses this deliberately — [admin_account_repair.rs](crates/pds/src/routes/admin_account_repair.rs) won't mint a reset token for a passwordless account, on the reasoning that it bootstraps a login path a key-sovereign account intentionally lacks. The user-facing email flow has no such guard. Setting a password gets you logged in today, at the cost of adding a phishable credential to an identity that didn't have one.

## Should did:web get sovereign sessions?

**Yes, and the pieces are already half-built — but only for one of the two did:web shapes.** The blocker isn't philosophy, it's that your specific account's DID document has no key you hold.

For *newly minted* did:web, ADR-0022 already mandates the anchor, and [create_did.rs:443](crates/pds/src/routes/create_did.rs:443) enforces it at promotion:

```rust
if !has_key("device", device_multibase) {
    return Err(... "did:web document does not publish the device key as #device");
}
```

and the wallet composes it — `composeDidWebDocument` in [did-web.ts:31](apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/did-web.ts:31) emits `#device` alongside `#atproto`.

**Your account never went through that path.** Migration-mode `createAccount` never inspects the document, and the hand-edited `malpercio.dev/.well-known/did.json` carries only `#atproto` (Custos-held) + `#atproto_pds`. So today there is no key in your DID document that you control — the only private key referenced by it lives on the PDS. A did:web sovereign session verified against that document would authenticate *Custos to itself*.

The design work is genuinely two decisions, and they're yours to make:

**1. What is the authority root for a did:web approval?** The natural answer is "a `#device` verification method in the document fetched live over HTTPS (SSRF-hardened client, never the `did_documents` cache)" — the structural mirror of "a key in the authoritative PLC rotation set, never the cached doc." That's a legitimate root, but weaker in kind: no tamper-evident log, no ordered key hierarchy, no 72-hour override. ADR-0022 already names that asymmetry ("`did:web` recovery is domain control plus escrowed keys") and insists method-specific paths stay gated so did:web never inherits PLC claims.

**2. What about Custos-hosted did:web?** This one has a real circularity problem. `POST /v1/did-web/document` ([did_web_hosting.rs](crates/pds/src/routes/did_web_hosting.rs)) lets an account rewrite its served document, authed by `authenticate_account_owner` — a **session token**. If sovereign-session verification then read that same served document, a stolen session could install an attacker `#device` key and mint "sovereign" sessions from it. For did:plc the equivalent attack is impossible: rewriting the rotation set requires a signature from an existing rotation key, and plc.directory is outside Custos entirely. My recommendation is to scope any did:web sovereign session to **self-hosted** documents only in v1, or require that the `#device` VM be immutable once set on a Custos-hosted doc.

**Recommendation for you specifically:** password reset now to unblock the OAuth login, and separately add a `#device` VM (your wallet device key) to `malpercio.dev/.well-known/did.json` so the account is ready the moment the server-side path exists. Adding it is harmless today — nothing reads it — and it's the prerequisite for ever dropping the password again.

Linear writes need the `plugin:linear:linear` MCP, which isn't authorized in this session — you'd need to connect it from an interactive session first. I can draft the issue body meanwhile, or write it up as a design plan in `docs/design-plans/` instead.

content.text:
Confirmed from your document — and that makes the gap much narrower than I described. Two useful details from it:

- `zDnae…` on both VMs is the multicodec `p256-pub` prefix, so `#device` is a P-256 key — exactly what `crypto::verify_did_key_signature` already accepts.
- `#device` (`zDnaeY2jnoij…`) is yours; `#atproto` (`zDnaexXYs4Ua…`) is the Custos-held repo signing key. That distinction turns out to be the whole security argument below.

## The change is one lookup, not a subsystem

I traced the full path. Signature verification in [sovereign_session.rs:148](crates/pds/src/routes/sovereign_session.rs:148) is already method-agnostic — it parses a `did:key:` URI and verifies P-256 or secp256k1. The *only* PLC-specific step is the authority lookup immediately after:

```rust
let plc = fetch_current_plc_state(&state.http_client, &state.config.plc_directory_url, &request.did).await?;
if !plc.rotation_keys.iter().any(|key| key == &request.signing_key) { ... }
```

[oauth_consent.rs:311](crates/pds/src/routes/oauth_consent.rs:311) has the identical shape. And the did:web counterpart primitive already exists — `resolve_web_did_document` ([resolution.rs:238](crates/pds/src/identity/resolution.rs:238)) does a live, SSRF-guarded, cache-bypassing HTTPS fetch of the document. That is the structural mirror of `fetch_current_plc_state`: authoritative source, never the cache.

The wallet side needs nothing. `sovereign_login_impl` ([sovereign_session.rs:181](apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/sovereign_session.rs:181)) never inspects the DID method — it resolves the per-DID device key, discovers the PDS, signs the canonical envelope. Point it at `did:web:malpercio.dev` today and it would produce a valid request that the server rejects at the gate.

So the feature is: extract `authorized_signing_keys(state, did) -> Result<Vec<String>, ApiError>` into `identity/` (both routes need it, and routes may not import each other), dispatch on method, delete the two `is_plc_did` gates.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
One non-obvious wrinkle: PLC stores `rotationKeys` as `did:key:z…` URIs, and the comparison above is plain string equality against `request.signing_key`. But a DID document's `verificationMethod` carries bare `publicKeyMultibase` (`zDnaeY2jnoij…`, no `did:key:` prefix). The did:web arm has to render `format!("did:key:{}", multibase)` before comparing, or every request fails with a confusing `signing_key_not_current_rotation_key`. Small, but it's the kind of thing that eats an afternoon.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Two decisions worth getting right

**1. Only `#device` counts — never "any verificationMethod."** Your document is the proof. `#atproto`'s private key lives on Custos. If the authority set were every VM in the document, Custos could sign its own sovereign-session envelope and mint a full-access session for your account with no key of yours involved. That inverts the entire point. `create_did.rs` already encodes this instinct for newly-minted did:web — it requires `#device` specifically ([create_did.rs:443](crates/pds/src/routes/create_did.rs:443)) — so scoping the authority set to `#device` keeps one rule across both paths.

**2. Custos-hosted did:web needs a gate; self-hosted doesn't.** `POST /v1/did-web/document` lets an account rewrite its own served document, authed by a **session token**. If verification then read that served document, a stolen session could install an attacker `#device` key and bootstrap "sovereign" sessions from it — a privilege escalation with no key compromise. did:plc has no such hole: rewriting the rotation set requires a signature from an existing rotation key, and plc.directory is outside Custos entirely.

Yours is self-hosted (the document is served from `malpercio.dev`, only `#atproto_pds` points at Custos), so you're unaffected either way — but the general feature isn't. My recommendation: resolve strictly via `resolve_web_did_document` (live fetch, never the cache — the cache is writable by that same route), and for Custos-hosted did:web either refuse sovereign sessions in v1 or make `#device` immutable once set.

## Answering the question you actually asked

Yes — did:web should have it, and ADR-0022 already implies it ("the document publishes the wallet device key alongside Custos's reserved `#atproto` key"). What ADR-0022 does *not* say is that anything consumes that key, and nothing does. It's currently a monitoring anchor and a promotion-time assertion, nothing more. The gate in `sovereign_session.rs` isn't a considered rejection of did:web — it's where the abstraction stopped, back when did:plc was the only method.

The honest caveat: this is weaker than the PLC version in kind, not just degree. Domain compromise is identity compromise, there's no tamper-evident log, and no 72-hour override. ADR-0022 already commits to that asymmetry, so the work is making sure the wallet's *language* around a did:web sovereign session doesn't inherit PLC's recovery promises.

## If you want it built

The interesting part is small enough that I'd rather you write it than me. I'd prepare `crates/pds/src/identity/authority.rs` with the shared plumbing — the did:plc arm lifted verbatim from the current code, the did:web fetch wired to `resolve_web_did_document`, the `did:key:` rendering handled, and both routes switched over — and leave the policy itself for you:

```rust
/// Which keys in a did:web document may authorize a sovereign session or an OAuth
/// consent approval for `did`.
///
/// Security-critical: `#atproto`'s private key is Custos-held, so including it would
/// let this server authenticate as the account it hosts.
fn did_web_authorized_keys(document: &Value, did: &str) -> Vec<String> {
    todo!()
}
```

Roughly 8 lines. The judgment calls in it are yours: whether to accept only the exact `{did}#device` id or any VM whose fragment is `device`; whether to require `type == "Multikey"` and `controller == did` the way `create_did.rs` does; and whether a document with *multiple* `#device`-shaped entries should authorize all of them or be rejected outright as malformed. That last one is the interesting one — permissive means a partially-compromised document still has a valid key in it, strict means a hand-edit typo locks you out of your own account.

Say the word and I'll set up the seam plus the test scaffold. Separately, I still can't file this in Linear — the `plugin:linear:linear` MCP needs authorizing from an interactive session — but I can draft the issue body or write it up as a design plan under `docs/design-plans/` alongside ADR-0022.

The `enable_managed_hosting` parameter is already wired into both the create and migrate flows, so all four ADR-0022 shapes are accessible. name: reference-linear-access
description: "How to read and write Linear (team MM / ezpds) from Claude Code — MCP for writes, API key for reads"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: bdaadf6b-adac-4639-958e-edc6feda2454
---

Linear team is **MM** ("Mal's Machinations"), project **ezpds**. Two access paths from Claude Code:

- **Writes** (status changes, comments, create/update issues): use the `plugin:linear:linear` MCP. It needs OAuth — on a fresh session only `mcp__plugin_linear_linear__authenticate` is loaded; call it, have the user authorize in the browser, then the real tools appear. `save_issue(id:"MM-98", state:"Done")` and `save_comment(issueId:"MM-98", body:...)` take identifiers directly; `state` accepts a name/type/ID.
- **Reads**: `LINEAR_API_KEY` is in `.env.local` (gitignored). `set -a; source .env.local; set +a` then POST GraphQL to `https://api.linear.app/graphql` with header `Authorization: $LINEAR_API_KEY`. Good for wave/label scans.

**Gotchas:**
- The `linear_wave_status` / `linear_list_issues` / `linear_update_issue` tools named in AGENTS.md are **Pi** extension tools (`.pi/extensions/linear/index.ts`), NOT available to Claude Code. Don't try to call them — replicate their GraphQL instead, or use the MCP.
- **Writes via Bash** (curl/python hitting the Linear API) are **hard-blocked** by the auto-mode classifier as external-system writes, even with user authorization. Writes must go through the authenticated MCP.
- zsh mangles `!` inside heredoc'd GraphQL (`String!` → `String\!`); inline values or put the query in a file written via the Write tool.
- The exhaustive `issues(first: 250)` wave-status scan can return HTTP 500; page smaller or filter by label (e.g. `labels: { name: { eq: "Wave 4: Repo + Blobs" } }`).
- **Wave labels are team-scoped to MM, not workspace-level.** `list_issue_labels` with NO `team` arg returns an incomplete set (only a few labels) — call it with `team:"MM"` to see the full wave list. Their real names carry a suffix: `Wave 0: Scaffolding`, `Wave 1: Running Server`, `Wave 2: Auth`, `Wave 3: Identity` AND `Wave 3: Key Sovereignty` (two Wave-3 labels), `Wave 4: Repo + Blobs`, `Wave 5: Federation`, `Wave 6: App Proxy`, `Wave 7: Hardening`, `Wave 8: auth.md`. `save_issue(labels:[...])` matches on the **exact full name** — `labels:["Wave 7"]` silently no-ops (returns `labels:[]`); use `"Wave 7: Hardening"`.

**Free-plan capacity (learned 2026-07-10):** the 250-issue cap counts only NON-archived issues — archiving frees quota, deletion is never needed (user deleted atbb issues needlessly before learning this). The Linear UI offers no manual archive and auto-archive waits ≥1 month after close, but the GraphQL `issueArchive` mutation archives immediately. A full local export (all 282 MM issues + comments) and a user-runnable archive script live in `linear-export/` in the repo (gitignored — repo is public, never commit it): `node linear-export/archive-done.mjs [--yes]`. Claude cannot run the archive script (Bash Linear writes blocked) — the user runs it.

Related: [[project_relay_cicd]].

content.text:
Memory corrected. On your plan — the three code decisions are right, and the fourth needs one change to actually be a security control.

## The three code decisions: yes

**Exact `{did}#device` only.** This is the one that matters most, and your own document shows why: `#atproto` (`zDnaexXYs4Ua…`) is Custos-held. Any policy admitting more than `#device` hands this server the ability to sign its own sovereign-session envelope for your account. Exact-id matching also makes the duplicate case degenerate — two VMs sharing an `id` is already a DID Core violation, so you're rejecting documents that were malformed regardless.

**Match `create_did.rs`'s predicate.** Agreed. One difference in shape worth knowing: `has_key` at [create_did.rs:432](crates/pds/src/routes/create_did.rs:432) *verifies* a key it already knows, so it compares `publicKeyMultibase` against an expected value. The authority lookup *discovers* the key, so it extracts that field instead. Same `type == "Multikey"` and `controller == did` checks, same id construction — just the last step inverted.

**Reject on multiple.** Fail-closed is correct here. You noted the trade-off yourself — a hand-edit typo could lock you out — but that failure is loud, recoverable by fixing the document, and doesn't touch the escrowed device key. The permissive alternative fails silently in the direction of "attacker key still works."

## The hosting decision: right call, wrong layer

Hiding the Custos-hosted shapes in the wallet is a sensible product decision. It is not a security boundary, and the plan currently treats it as one.

`enable_managed_hosting` is already a plumbed parameter on both flows — [migrate.rs:263](apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/migrate.rs:263) and [lib.rs:754](apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/lib.rs:754) — so hiding it means the wallet stops passing `true`. `POST /v1/did-web/hosting` remains a live, session-authed route on the server. Any client that isn't your wallet can still enable it, and any account that *already* enabled it stays enabled. If sovereign sessions ship without a server-side check, the circular path is open for those accounts regardless of what the wallet renders.

So: keep the wallet change (it's the right default), and add the gate in `did_web_authorized_keys` — refuse to return any key when `did_web_hosting_enabled_at IS NOT NULL`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The gate turns out to be exact rather than a heuristic, which is unusually clean. `POST /v1/did-web/document` already refuses unless hosting is enabled ([did_web_hosting.rs:135](crates/pds/src/routes/did_web_hosting.rs:135) — "Only edit the document Custos actually serves"). So `did_web_hosting_enabled_at IS NULL` isn't a proxy for "the doc can't be rewritten by a session token" — it *is* that condition, exactly. The two states line up with no gap in either direction, which means the gate can be justified in one sentence in the ADR rather than defended as a conservative approximation.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

That also gives you a clean upgrade path later: making `#device` immutable across a `/v1/did-web/document` edit would let you drop the gate and support all four shapes, without redesigning anything.

## One thing to check before I build

**Is `did:web:malpercio.dev` already flagged as Custos-hosted?** If that migration ran with `enable_managed_hosting = true`, `did_web_hosting_enabled_at` is set on your account row — and the gate we just agreed on would refuse sovereign sessions for the exact account you're trying to unlock. It's not externally observable (your DNS points at your own host, so Custos never serves the document even if the flag is on; the flag is pure DB state).

Two ways to settle it: `GET /v1/admin/accounts?q=malpercio` with your admin token, or a direct read of `did_web_hosting_enabled_at` on prod. If it *is* set, the fix is a one-line `{"enabled": false}` POST — you'd be turning off something that was never doing anything anyway.

## Proposed scope

Assuming that comes back NULL, here's what I'd build:

- `crates/pds/src/identity/authority.rs` — `authorized_signing_keys(state, did)`, dispatching did:plc → existing `fetch_current_plc_state` path, did:web → `resolve_web_did_document` (live fetch, never cache) + the `#device` policy + hosting gate.
- Delete the `is_plc_did` gates in [sovereign_session.rs:114](crates/pds/src/routes/sovereign_session.rs:114) and [oauth_consent.rs:252](crates/pds/src/routes/oauth_consent.rs:252); both switch to the shared lookup. Their existing `rejected()` / `approval_rejected()` helpers already collapse every failure to one opaque message, so no new enumeration surface.
- Wallet: stop offering the two Custos-hosted shapes.
- ADR-0022 amendment recording the `#device`-only policy, the hosting gate and its exactness, and the deferral.
- Changelog fragment (`changelog.d/`) — both routes are shipped surfaces, so the gate will demand one.

Want me to file this in Linear (team MM, project ezpds, Wave 3: Key Sovereignty seems right) and start on it? And do you want me to write the `did_web_authorized_keys` policy body given you've now specified it precisely, or still leave that one for you?

content.text:
No — that field isn't returned. `AdminAccountRow` ([accounts.rs:901](crates/pds/src/db/accounts.rs:901)) carries exactly `did`, `handle`, `created_at`, `lifecycle`, `blob_bytes`, `flagged`, and `did_web_hosting` has zero occurrences in either `accounts.rs` or [admin_list_accounts.rs](crates/pds/src/routes/admin_list_accounts.rs). Your output is the complete row — it tells us nothing about the flag either way.

## Two ways to actually read it

**Direct DB read** (definitive):

```bash
railway run --service pds sqlite3 "$EZPDS_DATA_DIR/pds.db" "SELECT did_web_hosting_enabled_at FROM accounts WHERE did = 'did:web:malpercio.dev';"
```

**Or probe it through the API**, which works if getting a shell is annoying. `POST /v1/did-web/document` checks hosting *before* it validates the document, and both checks are before any write:

```
authenticate → require_did_web → hosting check (:135) → `id` present (:148) → `id` matches (:149) → rewrite (:158)
```

So sending `{"document": {}}` with your owner credential fails at `:135` with `"managed did:web hosting is not enabled for this account"` if the flag is NULL, or at `:148` with `"document is missing an \`id\`"` if it's set. Two distinct messages, and the request cannot mutate anything — it dies four lines before `rewrite_did_document`. The catch is that this route wants account-owner auth (wallet session or full-access token), not your admin token, so the DB read is probably less work.

## This gap is worth closing

The operator console can't see whether an account is Custos-hosted at all. That's a mild annoyance today and a real one the moment this flag starts gating sovereign sessions — you'd have an account silently refused a login path with no way to see why from the admin surface. Adding `didWebHosting: bool` to the listing row is a few lines (one more correlated scalar in the existing per-row subquery pattern) and I'd fold it into the same change rather than filing it separately.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
Worth noticing *why* the field was never there: the listing was built around lifecycle, storage, and moderation flags — the things an operator acts on. `did_web_hosting_enabled_at` was, until this conversation, a pure serving toggle with no security meaning, so it had no reason to surface. Promoting it to an auth gate changes its category, and the observability has to follow. That's the general shape of the risk here: the gate is cheap to add and easy to forget to make visible.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

One unrelated thing I noticed in your row: `totalBytes: 0`. That's blob bytes only, so it's correct if the account has no media — but if you expected images or video to have come across in the migration, that's worth a second look at the blob drain leg independently of any of this.

Once you've read the flag, tell me what it says and I'll file the Linear issue and start on `did_web_authorized_keys` — including whether you want to write the policy body yourself.

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack**, trace backward:
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use ed3d-plan-and-execute:test-driven-development for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultrathink this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Integration with Other Skills

**This skill requires using:**
- **test-driven-development** - REQUIRED for creating failing test case (see Phase 4, Step 1)

**Complementary skills:**
- **coding-effectively** - Includes `defense-in-depth` for adding validation at multiple layers
- **verification-before-completion** - Verify fix worked before claiming success

## Real-World Impact

From debugging sessions:
- Systematic approach: 15-30 minutes to fix
- Random fixes approach: 2-3 hours of thrashing
- First-time fix rate: 95% vs 40%
- New bugs introduced: Near zero vs common

Phase 1 findings. I'm not proposing a fix yet — the evidence doesn't yet distinguish two very different situations.

## What `totalBytes: 0` actually means

Every blob read path an operator can reach reads the **same table**, `blob_owners`:

| Surface | Query source |
|---|---|
| admin `totalBytes` | `blob_owners JOIN blobs` ([accounts.rs:971](crates/pds/src/db/accounts.rs:971)) |
| `GET /v1/accounts/:id/storage` | identical SQL ([blobs.rs:110](crates/pds/src/db/blobs.rs:110)) |
| `com.atproto.sync.listBlobs` | `list_blob_cids` → `blob_owners` ([blobs.rs:435](crates/pds/src/db/blobs.rs:435)) |
| `com.atproto.repo.listMissingBlobs` | `present_cids` → `blob_owners` ([blobs.rs:224](crates/pds/src/db/blobs.rs:224)) |
| `com.atproto.sync.getBlob` | ownership-scoped `get_owned_blob` |

So `totalBytes: 0` tells us precisely one thing: **there are no `blob_owners` rows for your DID.** It says nothing about whether the bytes exist on disk — and neither will `listBlobs` or `listMissingBlobs`, which will both report "nothing / everything missing" from the same empty table.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
This is the sharpest thing the investigation turned up, independent of your case: there is **no operator-reachable read path that distinguishes "ownership rows lost" from "bytes destroyed."** The physical `blobs` table and the filesystem are only ever consulted through an ownership join. `blob_scrub` walks the directory for orphans, but by its definition an orphan is a file with no `blobs` row — and `blob_gc` deletes the physical row and the file together when the last owner goes, so that path never catches this. Diagnosing this at all required a DB shell.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Also: bsky rendering your images is not evidence

Blob embeds are served from `cdn.bsky.app`, which caches aggressively and independently of your PDS. Images can render in the app long after the origin lost the bytes. I'd set that observation aside entirely as a signal.

## Two hypotheses, one decisive query

Your account's `createdAt` is `2026-07-25 01:51:43` — hours old.

**H-A (benign, and I think more likely):** this account row is *new* — re-migrated or re-created today — and the blob drain leg didn't run or didn't complete against this row. Blobs were never in this row's ownership, nothing was lost, and the drain simply needs re-running.

**H-B (a real bug):** the drain ran, but the ownership rows aged out and GC reclaimed them. The mechanism is concrete. `uploadBlob` stamps every new ownership row with `temp_until = now + temp_ttl_secs` (default **6 hours**, [config.rs:486](crates/common/src/config.rs:486)). Only `blob_gc`'s reconcile makes a row permanent, and it does that by walking the MST — but `collect_referenced_blob_cids` returns an **empty map, not an error**, when `repo_root_cid IS NULL` ([blob_gc.rs:225](crates/pds/src/blob_gc.rs:225)). An account with uploaded blobs is a GC candidate via `blob_owners` regardless of whether it has a repo ([blobs.rs:260](crates/pds/src/db/blobs.rs:260)). So blobs uploaded to a repo-less account look unreferenced on every pass, their 6-hour clock runs out, and the sweep deletes the ownership row, the physical row, and the file. GC runs every 30 minutes.

The standard migration order (importRepo → drain) is safe from this. An interrupted, reordered, or retried migration is not.

Three queries settle it:

```bash
railway run --service pds sqlite3 "$EZPDS_DATA_DIR/pds.db" "SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM blobs WHERE account_did='did:web:malpercio.dev'), (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(size_bytes),0) FROM blobs WHERE account_did='did:web:malpercio.dev'), (SELECT repo_root_cid FROM accounts WHERE did='did:web:malpercio.dev'), (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM blob_owners WHERE account_did='did:web:malpercio.dev');"
```

- **Physical count > 0, owners = 0** → bytes are intact, ownership was lost. Recoverable, and reconcile should even re-adopt them on its next pass once the repo references them (`upsert_owner_referenced` adopts referenced-but-unowned stored blobs).
- **Both 0, `repo_root_cid` set** → H-B is live; the bytes are gone from the DB. Next question is whether `[blob_mirror]` is configured in prod, because the bucket copy plus Litestream are then the recovery path.
- **Both 0, `repo_root_cid` NULL** → the migration didn't complete at all; re-run the drain.

Give me that row and I'll take it from there. Holding off on any code until we know which of these we're in — including the `didWebHosting` flag addition, which I'd rather land in the same change as whatever observability this turns out to need.

`restore_blob_backup(did)` walks the manifest and `uploadBlob`s each file back, and the module notes it's **trustless — restored bytes re-hash to the same CID, so records never need rewriting** ([blob_backup.rs:6](apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/blob_backup.rs:6)). Your `repo_root_cid` is set and those records reference the blob CIDs, so the next GC pass (≤30 min) pins every restored blob permanent. You are not re-arming the trap.

## Don't count on the mirror

If `[blob_mirror]` is configured, it likely won't help: a bucket key whose `blobs` row is gone is deleted on the next pass ([blob_mirror/mod.rs:27](crates/pds/src/blob_mirror/mod.rs:27)). The refusal tripwire only fires when the `blobs` table is *wholly* empty, which it isn't on a multi-account server. Worth a bucket listing before assuming, but plan around iCloud.

## The part that ties back to the did:web thread

`SessionProvider::full_access_client` is "the seam every authenticated wallet operation on a Custos-hosted identity goes through" ([session_provider.rs:12](apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/session_provider.rs:12)). Its ladder is: valid access JWT → refresh via `refreshSession` → **`NeedsUnlock` → biometric sovereign login**. And `restore_blob_backup` sits on that seam, with its own `SessionExpired` variant telling the frontend to "run the biometric sovereign login and retry (restore only)" ([blob_backup.rs:74](apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/blob_backup.rs:74)).

Sovereign login is the thing the server refuses for `did:web`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
So the recovery path for this account is alive **only while the refresh chain from the migration survives**. When it lapses, the wallet hits `NeedsUnlock`, sovereign login 401s on the `is_plc_did` gate, and the restore becomes unreachable — for an account whose only other credential is a password it doesn't have. The gate we started this conversation discussing as a login inconvenience is actually sitting between you and your own backup. That's a much stronger argument for the did:web authority work than "OAuth is annoying," and it also argues for keeping a password set on this account until that ships, purely as a second key to the door.

**So: run the restore while the session still works.** That's the one time-sensitive action here.

Recovery doesn't depend on this, but whether there's a defect to fix does. The two candidates remain "GC swept them" versus "the drain never completed against this account row," and the logs settle it:

```bash
railway logs --service pds | grep -E "blob GC pass complete|deleted bucket object"
```

A pass with `deleted > 0` around the migration window confirms GC reclaimed them and there's a real bug: the sweep in `run_blob_gc` is global (`list_expired_temp_owners` across all accounts) and isn't gated on whether that account's reconcile succeeded, so a repo-less or reconcile-failing account's fresh uploads age out and get destroyed.
